title: Lawrence Brown's solo, Jimmy Nottingham, and how the album saved Atlantic
summary: On day two Leeman recommends Jimmy Nottingham when trumpeter Joe Newman is missing, and Ahmet Ertegun later says the album rescued Atlantic Records from receivership.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: One of the outstanding things was on that date was

Lawrence Brown's trombone playing behind the side "Morning Glory" -- behind Joe Turner when he sang; it was -- another two things I'd like to call to attention is the second day, there was a two day date, and we went back and I had set up, and they were still waiting, they were starting late on the date -- they were waiting for a trumpet player. There might have been a mixup, but Joe Newman wasn't there, and they didn't know what to do.

Well, I had just finished a Hit Parade rehearsal, and gone over to that date, and it dawned on me that one of my dear friends on the Hit Parade, who had also worked with Count Basie, was Jimmy Nottingham, so I said, "Gee, I think, if you're stuck, why don't you call Jimmy Nottingham and see if he's there, and he'll come over" -- because everybody goes for a little taste after rehearsal. Well, they did. They called and they got Jimmy Nottingham. And when this record was released, Jimmy Nottingham was so indebted to me that he was included on that great date, that over the years, I never could buy a drink around him, and Jimmy just passed away this past year, and I won't forget his work on this album -- he's listed on the back as contributing, "I Want a Little Girl" -- it says Jimmy Nottingham replaces Joe Newman on trumpet and Seldom Powell replaced Frank Wes on tenor sax.
And the final sum up of this record, this album,

was that Ertegun, the owner of Atlantic Records, has told me since then, in all sincerity, that they were just about to go under bankruptcy the time -- Atlantic Records -- he owned Atlantic Records with his brother, Nesuhi Ertegun, who also supervised that date.

And he told me that they were going in a receivership, and this one album bailed him out completely, and put them back on their feet and they went on -- after that, I believe they had such artists as Ella Fitzgerald and they climbed and went on to great heights, and this is one of the biggest recording companies of all time at this day and age.
Of course, they're in all other things -- modern rock and pop and so forth now.
